tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

[Normal] BAYLOR HEALTH AND WELLNESS
[Normal] Applied Performance
[Normal] Annual Report 2024-2025
[Normal] Prepared by:
[Normal] Eric Rash
[Normal] Director of Applied Performance
[Normal] Date: October 2025
[Heading 1] Table of Contents
[Heading 1] EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
[Heading 2] Department Mission Statement
[Body Text] Drive the elite performance of championship-level athletic programs by leveraging science and technology through education and relationships.
[Heading 2] Key Achievements 2024/2025
[List Paragraph] Scaled Data Collection and Athlete Monitoring by 60% - Collected 1,000+ data sessions across eight platforms, enabling evidence-based training decisions and injury risk mitigation across the athletic department.
[List Paragraph] Grew relationship within HHPR to lay the groundwork for future research initiative. Helping with the publication for peer-reviewed research, in collaboration with HHPR, integrating PhD students into athletics operations, and co-authoring two peer-reviewed publications
[List Paragraph] Implemented Advanced Performance Technologies Across Multiple Sports - Successfully deployed ForceFrame muscle force testing and Kinexon player tracking systems in Fall 2024, serving Football, Men's and Women's Basketball, and Olympic Sports programs, providing previously unavailable objective metrics that enhanced return-to-play protocols, workload management, and data-driven communication with coaching and medical staff.
[Heading 2] Strategic Vision
[Body Text] We will serve as a project-based group, without specific sport assignments. Instead, the department will consist of content matter experts serving the following areas: biomechanics, exercise physiology, performance technology, and data science.
[Body Text] Our objective will be to solicit questions from key stakeholders to address specific needs and/or unique questions that arise throughout the season/year.
[Body Text] The Applied Performance department will operate within three primary service areas:
[List Paragraph] Student-athlete and staff education.
[List Paragraph] Performance, data analytics, and planning.
[List Paragraph] Research and development.
[Heading 1] SECTION 1: YEAR IN REVIEW
[Heading 2] 1.1 Performance Metrics & Analytics
[Heading 3] Quantitative Impact
[Heading 2] 1.2 Success Stories & Case Studies
[Heading 3] Case Study 1: Facility Transition
[Body Text] Sport: Football
[Body Text] Challenge: Team transitioned from afternoon to morning practices in a new facility, raising concerns about potential decreases in practice intensity and quality with the schedule change.
[Body Text] Intervention: Conducted GPS analysis comparing key performance metrics before and after the transition. Implemented weekly Thursday practice top-ups to ensure athletes achieved ≥90% maximum velocity efforts before competition.
[Body Text] Outcome: Data revealed no drop-off in practice intensity during morning sessions. Athletes demonstrated equal or improved speed metrics in the new timeframe. Thursday top-ups ensured that 100% of athletes met the 90% max velocity threshold each week, validating the schedule change and establishing a sustainable training model.
[Heading 3] Case Study 2: Load Monitoring Implementation
[Body Text] Sport: Volleyball
[Body Text] Challenge: Lack of objective data to identify periods where competition schedule demands and weekly training load were misaligned, potentially increasing injury risk and compromising athlete readiness.
[Body Text] Intervention: Implemented session RPE (sRPE) tracking throughout the season, converting responses into training load scores. Monitored data weekly to identify high-load periods and schedule training misalignments and used findings to advocate for practice modifications during congested competitive windows.
[Body Text] Outcome: Successfully identified multiple periods of load-schedule misalignment during the season. Data-driven insights enabled the strength coach to secure practice modifications, better managing the athlete workload. Post-season analysis quantified sRPE-training load relationships, providing coaching staff with evidence-based frameworks for future season planning and load management strategies.
[Heading 2] 1.3 Technology & Innovation Implementations
[Heading 3] New Technologies Deployed
[Body Text] Force Frame
[Body Text] Implementation Date: Fall 2024
[Body Text] Sports Utilizing: Football, Basketball (M/W), Olympic Sports
[Body Text] Impact: ForceFrame muscle force testing has enhanced our athlete monitoring and return-to-play protocols by streamlining assessment efficiency and providing previously unavailable objective force metrics. Technology has improved decision-making on training modifications, return-to-play timelines, and load management, providing coaching and medical staff with quantifiable data to guide athlete readiness and recovery across multiple sports.
[Body Text] Kinexon
[Body Text] Implementation Date: Fall 2024
[Body Text] Sports Utilizing: Women's Basketball
[Body Text] Impact: Kinexon player tracking has transformed our approach to athlete monitoring by quantifying practice volume, intensity, and density across training sessions. The system provides objective metrics for athlete profiling and return-to-play protocols, enabling data-driven decisions around workload management and readiness. These insights have enhanced communication with coaching staff, supporting evidence-based adjustments to practice design and individualized load management strategies.
[Heading 3] Data Integration Achievements
[Body Text] Our department has integrated multiple data streams, including player-tracking metrics, force assessments, subjective load monitoring, and performance testing, to create a comprehensive athlete-monitoring system. This integrated approach enables cross-referencing of external training loads with internal responses and neuromuscular status, providing a holistic view of athlete readiness.
[Heading 1] SECTION 2: DEPARTMENT OPERATIONS
[Heading 2] 2.1 Organizational Structure
[Body Text] Director of Applied Sport Science: Eric Rash
[Body Text] Credentials: MS, SCCC, CPSS (Pursuing)
[Body Text] Areas of Expertise: Strategic vision, vendor relations, Innovation, and Research initiatives
[Body Text] Professional Development: Annual Catapult Football Workshop, PCA Data Analysis online course, Power BI for Strength Coaches level 1, Power BI for Sport Science level 1 and 2
[Body Text] Applied Performance Specialist: AJ Tademy
[Body Text] Credentials: MS, CSCS, CPSS (Pursuing)
[Body Text] Areas of Expertise: Logistical support and system operations
[Body Text] Professional Development: CSCS certification, Power BI for Sport Science, level 1 and 2 (Sport Horizons)
[Body Text] Undergraduate Interns: 1 (Andrew McKowen)
[Heading 2] 2.2 Service Delivery Model
[Heading 3] Core Services
[Body Text] Performance Testing & Assessment
[Body Text] Performance testing is integrated into scheduled lifting sessions to monitor physical development and readiness. Force plate assessments are conducted weekly for most teams to track neuromuscular function and jump performance. 
[Body Text] Mid-thigh pull testing is performed weekly to monthly, depending on the sport and season phase, to evaluate maximal force production. This testing frequency balances longitudinal data collection with minimal disruption to training, enabling trend analysis and informed programming decisions throughout the year.
[Body Text] Training Load Monitoring
[List Paragraph] Comprehensive multi-device monitoring ecosystem to track athlete training load and readiness across 14 sports. The department collected 1000+ data sessions across eight platforms. This centralized data-collection approach enables evidence-based training decisions, load management, and injury-risk mitigation across the athletic department.
[Body Text] Data Analytics & Reporting
[List Paragraph] Regular performance reports and dashboards utilizing data from multiple platforms to inform coaching decisions and track athlete development.
[List Paragraph] Analytics deliverables support daily training decisions, weekly load management, and longitudinal performance tracking.
[Body Text] Research & Innovation
[Body Text] Actively engaged with HHPR on several different initiatives. Most center on traditional research projects that lead to publication.
[Body Text] Beyond the active research taking place, Athletics staff serve as adjunct faculty in the spring semester, instructing the course HP5355
[Heading 1] SECTION 3: RESEARCH & INNOVATION
[Heading 2] 3.1 Academic Partnerships
[Heading 3] Robbins College: HHPR
[Normal] Collaborative Projects: Baseball Oura ring sleep study; Acrobatics and Tumbling Projects (Various)
[Normal] Student Involvement: Participation from multiple varsity sport programs (A&T, Baseball)
[Normal] Key Outcomes:
[Body Text] Acrobatics and tumbling - Injury Profile: 22 athletes sustained 28 injuries (11 missed time) - primarily lower extremity, soft-tissue, non-contact injuries from tumbling (50%) Nutritional Deficiencies: 73% developed low iron levels (<35 ng/ml), 20.8% consumed insufficient calories, and carbohydrate intake was inadequate (especially among bases) Health Concerns: 17% reported secondary amenorrhea (higher prevalence in tops), indicating potential energy availability issues despite significant increases in fat-free mass and reduced alcohol consumption
[Body Text] Baseball – Sleep Metrics: Athletes averaged 7.3 hours of sleep with 89% sleep efficiency during fall training. Positive Performance Associations: Higher sleep efficiency, more nights with 7+ hours of sleep, and more nights with >90% sleep efficiency were all linked to greater improvements in force plate power output. Negative Performance Impact: Increased nighttime awakenings were negatively associated with power output improvements, indicating sleep quality disruption hindered performance gains
[Heading 2] 3.2 Publications & Presentations
[Heading 3] Peer-Reviewed Publications
[Body Text] Pickler, M. C., Funderburk, L. K., Lee, K. M., Bolden, L. K., Heileson, J. L., Rash, E. R., & Gallucci, A. R. (in press). Development of altered iron status following pre-season training in NCAA Division-I female acrobatics & tumbling athletes. Journal name not specified.
[Body Text] Pickler MC, Gallucci AR, Lee KM, Bolden LK, Rash ER, Tinsley GM*. Body Composition Changes in NCAA Division I Female Soccer Players Throughout Collegiate Playing Career. J Strength Cond Res. May 2025.
[Heading 1] SECTION 4: UNIT GOALS & OBJECTIVES
[Heading 2] 4.1 Goals for 2025/2026
[Heading 3] Goal 1: Student-Athlete and Staff Education
[Body Text] Objective: Implement and optimize education programming (Performance School for staff and Performance Academy for student-athletes) to enhance sport science knowledge and application across the athletics department.
[Body Text] Key Result Indicators:
[List Paragraph] Launch four core Performance School modules (Performance Technologies, Planning and Monitoring, Load Prescription, Return-to-Play Protocols)
[List Paragraph] Develop and implement three Performance Academy topics for student-athletes (Sleep Optimization, Travel Preparation, Recovery Strategies)
[Body Text] Timeline:
[List Paragraph] Q1 (Fall Semester): Complete module development and launch
[List Paragraph] Q2-Q4: Ongoing optimization and refinement
[Body Text] Resources Required:
[List Paragraph] Subject matter experts for curriculum development
[List Paragraph] Learning management system or platform
[List Paragraph] Staff time for implementation and delivery
[Heading 3] Goal 2: Analytics and Planning of Sport-Related Data
[Body Text] Objective: Optimize data-driven decision-making by centralizing data management and implementing a robust analytics platform to replace current systems.
[Body Text] Key Result Indicators:
[List Paragraph] Establish a centralized data storage system with secure access for three distinct user groups by year-end
[List Paragraph] Migrate >50% of data from Excel to new database structure
[List Paragraph] Complete evaluation and cost analysis of at least two analytics platform replacements
[Body Text] Timeline:
[List Paragraph] Q1: Establish data infrastructure and access protocols
[List Paragraph] Q2: Evaluate analytics solutions and conduct a comparison
[List Paragraph] Q3-Q4: Data migration and platform implementation
[Body Text] Resources Required:
[List Paragraph] Database infrastructure and IT support
[List Paragraph] Analytics platform licenses
[Heading 3] Goal 3: Research and Development
[Body Text] Objective: Advance sports science research to improve athletic performance while fostering collaborative relationships with the Health, Human Performance, and Recreation (HHPR) department and engaging student researchers.
[Body Text] Key Result Indicators:
[List Paragraph] Develop at least three research questions leveraging existing datasets in collaboration with HHPR
[List Paragraph] Co-author one research paper with HHPR faculty or graduate students
[List Paragraph] Implement findings from at least one research project into practical training protocols
[Body Text] Timeline:
[List Paragraph] Q1 (Fall Semester): Establish HHPR collaboration, develop research questions, initiate literature review on return-to-play practices
[List Paragraph] Q2: Establish Sport Science Think Tank, develop Sport Science database
[List Paragraph] Q3: Research dissemination and internship engagement
[List Paragraph] Q4: Implementation of findings and protocol development
[Body Text] Resources Required:
[List Paragraph] HHPR faculty collaboration time
[List Paragraph] Research database and tracking systems
[List Paragraph] Return-to-play outcomes tracking infrastructure
[List Paragraph] Cross-departmental coordination and meeting space
--TABLE 0
Metric | 2023/24 | 2024/25 | % Change
Performance Assessments | 5 | 7 | +40%
Load Management Reports | 50+ | 100+ | +100%
Technology Touchpoints | 500+ | 800+ | +60%
Research Projects | 8 | 10 | +25%

---
name: kenny-boyd-writing-voice
description: "How Kenny Boyd (Exec Sr Assoc AD, SA Services) writes and leads — post template, tics, bad-news pattern, what he values; use when writing to him, for him, or in his voice"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: b0bad54c-c508-4189-9898-0dd8063d93ae
  modified: 2026-10-06T14:03:59.894Z
---

Source: SA Services Leadership channel export (19 agendas 9/2025–3/2026), 11 Teams
posts 3/27–10/5/2026, and 96 emails from Kenny to Eric (10/2025–10/5/2026), reviewed
2026-10-06.

**Two registers.** Agendas: bare outlines, two-sided slogans ("Thermostat vs.
Thermometer", "Anger vs. Apathy", "Be Present"), questions as prompts ("Why are we doing
___?"), a running "What I'm working on…" list repeated weekly. Posts: warm prose that
explains the reason for every ask.

**Post template.** Bold label-first title (PLEASE REVIEW: / ASSISTANCE NEEDED: /
REMINDER: / Article Review:), banner for big items → @team + one purpose sentence →
numbered asks to a role ("Unit Leads - Please…") → why → his travel/OOO dates → thanks.

**Tics.** Numbers in parentheses "(3) weeks", "(38)". Ellipses as hand-off ("Let us know
on this thread…"). Long sentences, typos left in — writes fast, substance over polish.
"We/us" by default; "I" when taking ownership. CAPS/bold only for rules with
consequences ("DO NOT PARK"). Light self-deprecating humor ("do forget (like I have)").

**Faith.** Woven in as allusion ("for such a time as this"), weekly Scripture + leadership
quote in fall 2025 agendas, "Spiritual Wellness day", prayer question in athlete survey.

**Bad-news pattern (4/30 Athletes.org post).** State headline neutrally → "dig into the
details" (asks sample size) → numbered context → concede ("We certainly can improve") →
name who owns it (Doug, Jovan, Dave Harper) → close on pride and mission. Defends team
without dismissing the criticism.

**Values.** Prep before meetings (bullets in advance). Lead time upward: internal
deadline well before the official one, so Doug/President have room. Explicit about who
sees what (Real Response access list). Good-neighbor framing; reframes constraints as
fortune. Protects staff time and well-being. Personnel requests go to him first, keep
him copied. Prefers subtraction over adding process. Skeptical of low-n surveys
("number of participants matter significantly").

**Email specifics.** Subject labels: FOR REVIEW / RESPONSE REQUESTED / PLEASE RESPOND
SEPARATELY / FEEDBACK REQUESTED. Says exactly how to reply (reply all, separately,
text). Closes loopholes in asks ("(3) challenges; if personnel is one, give (3)
others"). Acks are one line ("Received. Thank you"). Credits people by name, often
including partner offices ("would not have been possible without…"). Tailors one
announcement for different audiences. To vendors: courteous, states his authority, makes no commitment.
Hospitality is a core value ("Unreasonable Hospitality" book for new staff).

**With Eric specifically.** Assigns work as "Coach Rash," with a deliverable, a deadline
and his review window ("by EOD Friday so I can review over the weekend"), with constraints
stated up front. Replies "great starting point" and then edits it himself. Asks scoping
checks on numbers ("only health and wellness research?"). Wants documents going upward
formalized and comprehensive ("include ALL areas"), traceable to external standards
(map the NCAA Perf Tech components in an appendix), and fitting existing ITS/campus
workflows rather than parallel ones. Approves with conditions (get the coach and AT to
sign off) and always "keep me updated," especially on cross-office comms. Delegates
by relationship ("you can speak their language to ITS"). Since 10/1/26: weekly
30-minute project check-in with Eric through the fall.

**Spoken (Fireflies SA_Leadership_10052026).** Opens the meeting with a devotional tied to the
point in the semester (mid-semester "peaks and valleys", Psalm 121 + Wooden) and a
call for leaders to be "that calming force". Closes with a reflection and a spoken prayer. Talks
in long, circling sentences full of "you know / I think / kind of". Explains decisions
plainly ("I'll just say it plainly", e.g. BANC breakfast cut on budget and football
practice times). Key lines: "inviting feedback requires you to be prepared to act upon
it"; "if we're going to do it… say we're going to do it and say we did". He redirects new
initiatives into existing groups ("instead of adding something else"). Pulse: 82 =
17% participation; goal ~1/3; calls it "a trust building process"; warns that raw
survey data skews toward the disgruntled ("don't take it personally").
In small private groups he gets blunt and informal and sizes up stakeholders by how
he expects them to react. Databricks stance (10/5/26): sees it as possibly
the next step beyond Kitman; start with one team; bring in neutral interpreters
between the data and the sport; a per-sport "menu" of what data goes in; ROI including
NIL; willing to push from the top ("ignorance cannot be a reason to stop"). He grounds
Eric's enthusiasm ("get too carried away"); he's already sold on the vision and wants
governance, a small proof of concept and a plan for the people who resist.

**How to apply:** Writing to or for him, use his template; with bad news use his order
(context, concede, owner). Hit his internal deadline, not the official one. Don't
over-polish. Frame Applied Performance work against his five annual goals (11/10/25):
industry-leading division, campus partnership (the research team Eric leads), unit
leader development, service prioritization, student-athlete voice.

Related: [[kenny-boyd-doc-review-preferences]] [[status-report-sourcing]]

description: "Kenny Boyd's editorial constraints on Athletics policy/framework docs — no language implying past incompetence, no judgmental tier labels, name the seniority of reviewers"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

  originSessionId: 126c5de4-d928-4658-88d2-1922d2464a29
  modified: 2026-08-11T23:13:32.529Z
---

Kenny Boyd (reviewer on the Baylor Athletics Software and Technology Management
Framework) consistently pushes back on three things in draft policy language:

1. **No language that implies the department was previously incompetent.** He cut
   "so the department stops discovering it is in the final year of an agreement
   with no time to act" for exactly this reason. Rewrite as forward-looking
   capability ("advance visibility of contract end dates and the lead time to
   evaluate options"), not as a problem being fixed.
2. **No judgmental or ranking-flavored labels.** He rejected the Light / Standard /
   Elevated review tiers. Neutral, descriptive, escalating names work better —
   Level 1 Standard / Level 2 Enhanced / Level 3 Comprehensive Review. He floated
   Basic / Intermediate / Advanced, which reads as sophistication of the
   *technology* rather than depth of *review*.
3. **Name the seniority of the reviewer, not just the office.** For ITS he wanted
   it clear that a supervisory-level person with authority to commit resources is
   involved, not a line technician. Frame this as decision authority the request
   requires, never as competence of the staff.

He also wants Baylor branding carried through headers/footers and draft status
marked on every page.

**Why:** These are tone constraints, not content ones — the same facts land or
fail on phrasing. Getting them wrong costs a full review cycle.

**How to apply:** Before sending any Athletics policy or framework draft for his
review, scan for blame-implying rationale, ranking adjectives on process tiers,
and unqualified office names where seniority matters.

# Baylor Doc Style

The house look for Baylor Athletics Word documents, defined once.

`baylor_docstyle.py` is a single module. Document builders import it instead of
setting their own fonts, colours and spacing, so every document comes out
looking like the same department wrote it.

## Where the style comes from

Every measurement in the module was read out of:

```
~/DEV/SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework/deliverables/
    Software_and_Technology_Management_Framework_DRAFT.docx
```

Eric chose that document as the house look on 2026-08-30. Nothing in the module
is invented. **If the module and that document ever disagree, the document
wins** — re-measure it rather than adjusting to taste.

## When to use it

**Every document going to administration** (leadership, Kenny Boyd, Chris Ruf,
senior staff) is built with this module, using only its components and defaults
— no local font sizes, margins or hand-built tables (Eric, 2026-09-29). If the
content will not fit a page limit in house style, ask Eric whether to add pages
or cut content; do not shrink below the house sizes.

## Use

```python
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/Users/kristinarash/DEV/Baylor_Doc_Style")
from baylor_docstyle import BaylorDoc

d = BaylorDoc("Athletics Technology Inventory",
              deck="What the department runs, and who runs it.",
              status="Interim — collection open to 29 September 2026")

d.meta([["Status", "Interim"], ["Prepared by", "Applied Performance"]])
d.callout("Two deadlines, not one", "29 August was our own deadline...")
d.section("Coverage — who has responded")     # numbered automatically
d.subhead("Still outstanding")
d.para("Five units have yet to respond.")
d.bullets(["**Softball** — Trackman, about to be installed."])
d.numbered(["**Follow up with five units.** Golf (M), Tennis (M)..."])
d.quote("Everything we have has gone through ITS approval.")
d.table(["Unit", "Responses"], [["Football", 3]], numeric_cols=(1,))
d.note("A caveat, in small italic grey.")
d.small("A caption under a table.")
d.save("out.docx")
```

`**double asterisks**` mark inline bold in every text argument.

Section numbers are handed out in order, so inserting a section never means
renumbering the ones after it.

## What the style is

# What is actually in the Kinexon exports

Written against the FA26 camp block sitting in `Box/Kinexon/Session Downloads` as of
2026-08-02. Re-run `python -m kinexon.verify` after any new drop; it re-checks
everything claimed here.

## The block

Six practices over three days — two-a-days, 30 July to 1 August 2026. Sixteen athletes.

| # | Date | Type | Length | Squad jumps | Jumps/min |
|---|------|------|--------|------------:|----------:|
| 1 | Thu 30 Jul, am | Camp, Full | 3h 10m | 946 | 4.97 |
| 2 | Thu 30 Jul, pm | Camp, Serve & Pass | 1h 31m | 529 | 5.83 |
| 3 | Fri 31 Jul, am | Camp, Individual/Skills | 2h 40m | **1,780** | **11.13** |
| 4 | Fri 31 Jul, pm | Camp, Full | 3h 10m | 991 | 5.21 |
| 5 | Sat 1 Aug, am | Camp, Serve & Pass | 3h 46m | 943 | 4.17 |
| 6 | Sat 1 Aug, pm | Camp, Full | 1h 36m | 900 | 9.39 |

Practice 3 is the outlier: nearly twice the jumps of any other session, in the
second-shortest one. An "Individual/Skills" session producing the heaviest jump day of
the block is either the most important finding in here or a labelling problem — worth
confirming before it goes near a coach.

## The three export shapes

The drop folder holds 36 files in three different shapes, and the loader handles each:

| Shape | Files | Grain | Metrics |
|---|---|---|---|
| `roster_wide` | `Practice N/<POS>_N.csv` | one row per athlete per practice | 21 |
| `team_wide` | `FA26_Practices1-6.csv`, `Team Numbers 1-6.csv` | one row per practice, squad totals | 21 |
| `full_export` | `Test.csv` | one row per athlete per **drill** | 68 |

Notes that cost time to work out:

- **`Team Numbers 1-6.csv` and `FA26_Practices1-6.csv` are byte-identical.** Two names
  for one export.
- **All three XLSX files duplicate a CSV.** Two of them (`FA26_Practices1-6.xlsx`,
  `Practice 1/OPP_1.xlsx`) are not real spreadsheets — they are the semicolon CSV opened
  in Excel as a *comma* file, so each line got split on its unquoted commas
  (`Camp,Full` became two cells). The loader detects this and rejoins on the comma.
  Getting that wrong shifts every column by one and silently corrupts the load.
- **Kinexon appends a `Ø All players` row to each per-position file.** It is a *mean*,
  not a total. It is dropped on ingest; leaving it in inflates every squad figure by
  roughly 6–16%.
- **Session descriptions are hand-typed and inconsistent** — `FA26_7.30.26Practice1`,
  `FA26_7.31.26_Practice3`, `FA26_8.1.2026_Practice5`. The practice *number* is the only
  reliable session identity, so that is what the loader keys on.

## Practice 1 is exported at drill level — the others are not

`Test.csv` covers Practice 1 only, but Kinexon recorded each drill as its own session,
so it carries a within-practice breakdown the other five practices do not have. The
drill rows contain no reference to the parent practice; the loader reattaches them by
time containment (a drill belongs to the practice whose window encloses it).

Jump density by drill, Practice 1:

| Drill | Length | Jumps/min |
|---|---|---:|
| Box Drill | 7m | **26.76** |
| Hurricane | 10m | 12.35 |
| Correction Exchange | 20m | 11.41 |
| Bunch Drill | 35m | 6.63 |
| Whirlwind | 35m | 3.92 |
| Dynamic Warm Up | 12m | 1.92 |

A 7× spread between Box Drill and Whirlwind. The session total (946 jumps, 4.97/min)
hides all of it. **Exporting every practice this way is the single highest-value change
available to the data collection** — it is the difference between "yesterday was heavy"
and "the third drill is what made yesterday heavy".

## Metric coverage

21 metrics exist for all six practices; 47 more exist for Practice 1 only, because only
that practice was exported in full. Notably **`Jump Load (J)`, metabolic work, physio
load, and the accel/decel splits are Practice-1-only** — so any report built on jump
load in joules cannot yet run block-wide. `Mechanical Load` is the load metric that *is*
available everywhere.

|---|---|

| `VALD_Performance/` | ForceDecks monitoring pipeline (PowerShell, Python, MATLAB) that builds and refreshes the `VALD_Monitoring_Football` workbook from raw VALD Hub exports. Own `AGENTS.md` + `CLAUDE.md`. Git repo, created 2026-09-14 on Windows. |

| Folder | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Risk_Stratification_Engine/` | Risk stratification → own `CLAUDE.md` |
| `Risk_Exposure_Windows/` | **Archived 2026-10-03**, merged into Risk_Stratification_Engine. GitHub repo read-only; local copy in `~/DEV_archive_hold/2026-10-03/` until ~2026-11-02. Registry: `project-triage/portfolio.json`. |
| `Injury_Surveillance/` | Baylor Football injury surveillance, 2017-2025: season change in injury count and severity, position risk thresholds, Five Pillars prevention proposal. Own `AGENTS.md` + `docs/STATUS.md`. Git repo, pushed to erash11. Disk is the source of truth; the Claude cloud project `Injury Surveillance` is only a pointer. **`data/` holds athlete-identifiable health data — never paste into chat or any external service; gitignored.** |
| `PracticeIntensity/` | Practice intensity |
| `AppliedUtilization/` | Utilization analysis |
| `AT_Utilization_Benchmarks/` | Athletic training utilization benchmarks → own `CLAUDE.md` |

## Testing and profiling

| Folder | What it is |
|---|---|
| `S2_Evaluation/` | S2 Cognition evaluation → own `CLAUDE.md`; disk is the source of truth, the Claude cloud project is only a pointer. Program docs in `docs/program/`. Norms and threshold traps: `project_s2-cognition-analysis.md`. |
| `COG_S2_Position_Reports/` | S2 position-level reports |
| `CATES/` | Comprehensive Athletic Talent Evaluation System: four-pillar athlete and recruit evaluation, medical A-F grade layered over the weighted score, plus the executive ROI white paper. Own `CLAUDE.md` + `AGENTS.md` + `docs/STATUS.md`. Git repo, pushed to erash11. Disk is the source of truth; the Claude cloud project `Athlete Evaluation Framework` is only a pointer. Program docs in `docs/program/`. No athlete data in the repo: it goes to the primary storage drive, see `data/README.md`. |
| `Baseball_PerformanceProfiles/` | Baseball performance profiles |
| `DexaProject/` | **Moved out of `~/DEV` to Google Drive — Mac 2026-09-09, Windows 2026-09-17.** Mac path `~/Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-eric.rash11@gmail.com/My Drive/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/DexaProject`; Windows path `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\DexaProject` (same Drive folder). DEXA scanner exports. **Identifiable health data — never paste contents into chat, an artifact, or any external service. Not in git, not pushed anywhere.** |
| `Jump_Dash/` | **Archived 2026-10-03**, merged into ForcePlate_DecisionSystem. GitHub repo read-only; local copy in `~/DEV_archive_hold/2026-10-03/` until ~2026-11-02. Registry: `project-triage/portfolio.json`. |
| `Ath_Medicine/` | Athletic medicine → own `CLAUDE.md` |
| `RTP_ProgressReport/` | Force plate return-to-play progress reports for individual athletes; three report styles, JSX/HTML template rendered per athlete. Own `AGENTS.md` + `CLAUDE.md`. Git repo, created 2026-09-14 on Windows. A similarly named folder also sits at `RTP_WorkingGroup/RTP_ProgressREPORT/` — check which is current before editing either. |

## Notes

- Related research and the citation library live in `RESEARCH.md`.
- Staff-facing decks, curricula, and proposals live in `PROGRAM.md`.

V1 shipped and the Room Deviation finding is null. The pre-registered 1.5 SD flag (ADR
0008) flagged 10 of 15 linemen, but simulating a homogeneous room with no atypical
athlete by construction flags 69% at that threshold, central 90% interval 7 to 13. The
observed 10 sits inside that interval and carries no information. At stricter
thresholds the room is less extreme than chance. No lineman deviates from the room
beyond normal variation.

calibrated against a homogeneous-room null before use, because the statistic is a
maximum over nine categories.

## Where the project stands

V1 shipped and the Room Deviation finding is null. The pre-registered 1.5 SD flag (ADR
0008) flagged 10 of 15 linemen, but simulating a homogeneous room with no atypical
athlete by construction flags 69% at that threshold, central 90% interval 7 to 13. The
observed 10 sits inside that interval and carries no information. At stricter
thresholds the room is less extreme than chance. No lineman deviates from the room
beyond normal variation.

The threshold was deliberately not retuned. Any future flagging rule has to be
calibrated against a homogeneous-room null before use, because the statistic is a
maximum over nine categories.

What survives is at room level and is weak: within-category spread matches the general
population (mean SD 0.98), only visual learning approaches a difference from the
NFL-prospect norm (z=-0.40, p=0.009) and that does not survive Bonferroni correction
across nine comparisons, and the room composite sits at the 44th percentile.

Generated by `scripts/build.js`. One row per deck. The hero is the Insight slide's visual (slide 3). Uniqueness rule: no two decks share a hero layout, so no two share a hero layout + palette pair.

45 decks · no duplicate hero layouts or layout + palette pairs

| # | Topic | Category | Hero layout | Hero concept | Palette | Hook / takeaway / alignment |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | Thinking After Hard Practice | Contextual Engineering & Education Delivery | dip-recovery-curve | Two possible recovery paths after hard practice, without measured depth, duration or assigned causes. Illustrative, not data. | night (Night, monochrome) | small-figure-field / question-right / left |
| 02 | The 8-Second Filter | Contextual Engineering & Education Delivery | survival-curve | A 'still reading' curve that drops steeply in the first seconds, then flattens: people screen fast, then stay | baylor (Baylor green and gold) | question-only / split-columns / left |
| 03 | Notification Fatigue | Contextual Engineering & Education Delivery | diminishing-stack | A stack of six message bars hugging the right margin, each fainter than the last: attention per message falls as the count rises | sand (Warm stone and sand) | statement / question-only / left |
| 04 | The Flipped Classroom Model | Contextual Engineering & Education Delivery | swapped-timelines | Two timelines across before / in the meeting / after: the same two pieces of work, shifted so that using the content, not hearing it, happens in the room | slate (Cool slate and pale gold) | assume-vs-measured / centered / center |
| 05 | Environmental Learning | Contextual Engineering & Education Delivery | room-plan-callouts | A plain floor plan of a locker room, flush right, with three numbered touchpoints in the order an athlete walks through it: coming in, at the sink, going out | paper (Graphite and antique gold) | single-word / headline-rule-question / right |
| 06 | Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio | Recovery & Load Management | ratio-scale-band | A single ratio scale from 0.5 to 2.0: the familiar 'close to usual' band and the spike zone from 1.5 up | forest (Forest and bone) | figure-left / headline-rule-question / left |
| 07 | The Placebo Effect in Recovery | Recovery & Load Management | stacked-contribution-bar | One bar for how recovered an athlete feels, split into what the tool does and what belief adds; an illustrative split, not data | sage (Field green and cream gold) | single-word / question-right / right |
| 08 | Sleep Debt | Recovery & Load Management | cumulative-ledger-steps | An illustrative week as a ledger: each short school night steps the running sleep balance lower; sleeping in on the weekend steps it up only a little | mint (Deep green and mint) | small-figure-field / split-columns / left |
| 09 | Active Recovery vs. Complete Rest | Recovery & Load Management | decision-fork | One question (normal training fatigue, or something else?) splitting into two paths: move easy, or stop and bring in Athletic Medicine | charcoal (Charcoal and gold) | question-only / centered / center |
| 10 | Cold Exposure Timing | Recovery & Load Management | goal-timing-matrix | Two rows by goal (build strength / play again soon), each a line from the session to what comes next, with cold placed right after the session: it works against one goal and helps the other | gold (Umber and gold field) | assume-vs-measured / question-only / left |
| 11 | The "Whole Person" Load Model | Cross-Functional Integration | stacked-area-total | Training, academic and life load stacked across one semester: training stays flat, yet the total spikes at midterms and finals | baylor (Baylor green and gold) | small-figure-field / question-right / left |
| 12 | Shared Language Across Silos | Cross-Functional Integration | one-word-three-readings | The word 'load' in the center with three published readings beneath it: a force in newtons, the training dose and response, and the IOC's broad load including travel and stress | charcoal (Charcoal and gold) | single-word / centered / center |
| 13 | The Transition Buffer | Cross-Functional Integration | timeline-gap | Practice block bleeding in from the left, a 60-90 minute gap for food, fluid and a shower, then class: the gap is the subject, labeled as a planning rule rather than a tested number | forest (Forest and bone) | assume-vs-measured / question-only / left |
| 14 | Coordination Over Control | Cross-Functional Integration | hub-vs-mesh | Two small networks of the same five units: control routes everything through one hub; coordination connects the units to each other, with a connector in the middle that keeps the calendar | mint (Deep green and mint) | quote-right / split-columns / right |
| 15 | Core Themes That Cross Every Unit | Cross-Functional Integration | unit-theme-dot-matrix | Five units down the side, topics across: sleep, stress and time are filled for every unit, while each unit's specialty is filled only once. An illustrative map, not a survey | sand (Warm stone and sand) | question-only / headline-rule-question / left |
| 16 | Reframing Anxiety as Excitement | Mental Health & Performance Psychology | one-signal-two-labels | One arousal signal in the center (racing heart, quick breath) with two arrows to two readings of it: threat ('I'm not ready') or challenge ('I'm ready for this') | slate (Cool slate and pale gold) | single-word / question-right / left |
| 17 | Centering Cues | Mental Health & Performance Psychology | three-step-loop | Three small nodes in a row (breathe, cue word, act) with a return line from act back to breathe: the same reset, repeated after every mistake | night (Night, monochrome) | question-only / centered / center |
| 18 | Mental Health First Aid | Mental Health & Performance Psychology | see-say-refer-path | A path that starts off the left edge and runs through three small stops (notice, ask, connect) to a larger end point: Baylor's licensed mental health staff | paper (Graphite and antique gold) | statement / headline-rule-question / left |
| 19 | Athlete Identity & Life Balance | Mental Health & Performance Psychology | two-ring-comparison | Two rings hugging the right margin: one almost entirely 'athlete', one where athlete is the biggest part of a broader mix (student, friend and family, faith and interests) | gold (Umber and gold field) | small-figure-field / split-columns / right |
| 20 | The Supportive Conversation | Mental Health & Performance Psychology | say-instead-pairs | Three phrase pairs in two columns: what we tend to say ('Toughen up') and what helps more ('Thanks for telling me'), joined by a short arrow | sage (Field green and cream gold) | quote-right / question-only / left |
| 21 | Nutrient Timing Basics | Nutrition & Fueling | day-line-windows | One training day as a line from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.: a meal window 1-4 h before practice, the session itself, and a protein window in the 2 h after | sand (Warm stone and sand) | question-only / question-right / left |
| 22 | Hydration Beyond Water | Nutrition & Fueling | range-bar-single-figure | One sweat-sodium bar from 10 to 70 mmol per liter (ACSM), a dashed extension to 100 (NATA), and a single marked average of about 35 | baylor (Baylor green and gold) | assume-vs-measured / headline-rule-question / left |
| 23 | Travel Nutrition | Nutrition & Fueling | route-with-stops | A travel day as one route line from campus to the game with three planned stops: the packed bag, the meal ordered ahead, the hotel checked before the trip | night (Night, monochrome) | statement / split-columns / right |
| 24 | The Fueling Station | Nutrition & Fueling | shelf-elevation | A front view of a fueling-station shelf: three shelves, with the eye-level shelf holding the default choice and the others quieter | forest (Forest and bone) | single-word / centered / center |
| 25 | Body Composition Conversations | Nutrition & Fueling | three-questions-stack | Three large questions to ask before anyone is measured: why measure, who measures and sees it, what support comes with the number | charcoal (Charcoal and gold) | quote-right / question-only / left |
| 26 | HRV in 5 Minutes | Sport Science & Technology | dots-rolling-average | Four weeks of scattered morning readings with a calm seven-day average through them: one low morning barely moves the line; a run of low mornings does | mint (Deep green and mint) | statement / question-right / left |
| 27 | GPS Load Data | Sport Science & Technology | speed-threshold-scale | One speed axis with a common high-speed line at 12.3 mph, and two top speeds against it: the same line sits at 88% of an offensive lineman's top speed and 61% of a wide receiver's | gold (Umber and gold field) | quote-right / centered / center |
| 28 | Sleep Tracking | Sport Science & Technology | two-by-two-quadrant | What the athlete looks at (weekly patterns vs nightly scores) against how it leaves them (curious vs anxious): patterns with curiosity help; nightly scores with worry hurt | slate (Cool slate and pale gold) | question-only / split-columns / left |
| 29 | Force Plates | Sport Science & Technology | mirrored-bars-tolerance | Six test days of left-versus-right difference around a center line, with the athlete's usual swing shaded and a fixed 10% flag dashed: the flag fires on normal days; only one day falls outside her own range | paper (Graphite and antique gold) | small-figure-field / question-only / right |
| 30 | Data to Decision | Sport Science & Technology | narrowing-steps | Data, insight, decision and action as four centered lines that shorten at each step, with a feedback arrow from action back to data: the loop only closes when what we did goes back to athletes and coaches | sage (Field green and cream gold) | single-word / headline-rule-question / left |
| 31 | Peer-Led Education | Leadership & Culture | captain-role-bars | Four horizontal bars show the exact percentages selecting the captain as best leader in each role. Each value appears once; bar lengths share a zero-based 0-100% scale (Fransen et al. 2014). | forest (Forest and bone) | statement / question-only / right |
| 32 | Players-Only Meetings | Leadership & Culture | agenda-ladder | A narrow upright ladder of three rungs, climbed from the bottom: purpose, rules, close. The top rung, one action with one owner, is the one most often skipped. | sand (Warm stone and sand) | question-only / question-right / left |
| 33 | The Ministry of Presence | Leadership & Culture | season-calendar-dots | A fictional Baylor planning calendar across six named sports, August to April. Dots suggest staff visits; a ring marks a possible check-in. Not attendance records, disclosure data or a verified schedule. | mint (Deep green and mint) | single-word / centered / center |
| 34 | Consultant vs. Speaker | Leadership & Culture | spike-vs-sustained | Two small timelines across a season: the one-day speaker as a single spike of attention that fades, and the consultant as a lower, sustained line with a bump at each planned touchpoint. Illustrative shapes, not data. | baylor (Baylor green and gold) | assume-vs-measured / split-columns / left |
| 35 | Measuring Beyond Attendance | Leadership & Culture | kirkpatrick-staircase | Four steps rising left to right: reaction, learning, behavior, results, each with the one question it answers. Behavior is marked: it is the step most programs never measure. | gold (Umber and gold field) | small-figure-field / headline-rule-question / left |
| 36 | Chronotype and Training | Emerging / Wildcard Topics | offset-dual-curves | Two performance curves across the day, the early type peaking near noon and the late type near 8 p.m., with a 7 a.m. session marked where they sit furthest apart | charcoal (Charcoal and gold) | question-only / headline-rule-question / left |
| 37 | Gut-Brain Axis | Emerging / Wildcard Topics | two-node-channels | Gut and brain as two plain circles joined by three two-way channels: nerves, immune signals, chemical messengers | night (Night, monochrome) | single-word / question-only / center |
| 38 | Breathwork Techniques | Emerging / Wildcard Topics | evidence-lollipops | Five popular breathing claims as lollipops whose length is the depth of evidence behind them: slow breathing for calm is long, mouth taping is short | sage (Field green and cream gold) | assume-vs-measured / question-right / left |
| 39 | Social Media and Athlete Mental Health | Emerging / Wildcard Topics | dose-response-curve | A gentle curve of risk against daily hours, flat through moderate use and rising past about three hours, with what the evidence can and can't say set beside it | slate (Cool slate and pale gold) | small-figure-field / centered / left |
| 40 | AI in Sport Science | Emerging / Wildcard Topics | sort-two-columns | Four common uses sorted into 'useful now' and 'not there yet', each with the check that puts it there: estimates checked against real lifts and lab capture vs injury predictions never tested on new athletes | paper (Graphite and antique gold) | quote-right / split-columns / right |
| 41 | Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) | Nutrition & Fueling | energy-allocation-remainder | Two illustrative energy allocations: exercise leaves different amounts for body functions; no quantities or diagnostic threshold | sage (Field green and cream gold) | question-only / centered / center |
| 42 | Concussion Reporting Culture | Cross-Functional Integration | reporting-passage-barriers | An illustrative passage interrupted by pressure, then a clear passage to Athletic Medicine with explicit staff support | baylor (Baylor green and gold) | single-word / question-right / left |
| 43 | Exertional Heat Illness: Recognize and Escalate | Recovery & Load Management | urgent-response-bracket | Concerning changes during exertion gathered by one bracket into an urgent Athletic Medicine response; an illustrative recognition cue, not a diagnostic algorithm | charcoal (Charcoal and gold) | statement / split-columns / right |
| 44 | Measurement Error: Is the Change Real? | Sport Science & Technology | change-interval-null-line | An illustrative interval around a positive estimated change crosses a no-change line; uncertainty belongs to the change, not just one test score | forest (Forest and bone) | assume-vs-measured / question-only / left |
| 45 | Retrieval Practice: Make the Lesson Stick | Contextual Engineering & Education Delivery | recall-feedback-offset-handoff | An illustrative stepped handoff from closed slides to attempted recall to corrective feedback, with a later recall cue separated by a dashed gap | mint (Deep green and mint) | quote-right / headline-rule-question / left |

49:def word_pdf(docx_path, pdf_path, timeout=180):
50-    """Export the PDF through Word and return Word's page count.
51-
52-    Word is the authority: it is what the reader opens. None means Word could
53-    not be driven and the PDF was not refreshed.
54-    """
55-    docx_path, pdf_path = os.path.abspath(docx_path), os.path.abspath(pdf_path)
56-    if sys.platform == "darwin":
57-        # Word blocks on an invisible dialog if the app is not already open.
58-        cmd = ["osascript", "-e", '''
59-        tell application "Microsoft Word"
60-          open POSIX file "{docx}"
61-          set d to active document
62-          set n to (compute statistics d statistic statistic pages)
63-          save as d file name POSIX file "{pdf}" file format format PDF
64-          close d saving no
65-          return n
66-        end tell
67-        '''.format(docx=docx_path, pdf=pdf_path)]
68-        env = None
69-    elif sys.platform == "win32":
70-        # COM needs no open Word window. If Eric already has Word running, COM
71-        # attaches to it, so only quit when this build's document was the last.
72-        cmd = ["powershell.exe", "-NoProfile", "-NonInteractive", "-Command", r'''
73-        $ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
74-        $w = New-Object -ComObject Word.Application
75-        $w.DisplayAlerts = 0
76-        $d = $w.Documents.Open($env:BUILD_DOCX, $false, $true)

# Output Ledger — Shipped Artifacts

Running record of things that actually shipped: deliverables handed off, talks
given, pipelines gone live, decisions locked. One line each, newest first.
Maintained by the `/harvest` skill (every harvest appends here) and by hand.

This is also the career-facing proof-of-work record — the answer to "what have
you shipped?" should be readable straight off this page.

`Knowledge/` article.

| 2026-08-11 | S2 Cognition offensive line review | Pre-registered analysis of 15 linemen asking whether the S2 composite hides actionable cognitive variation. The gate passed — categories are only weakly related (r~0.18), so the composite does discard profile detail — but the finding is null: the 1.5 SD flag fired on 10 of 15, and null calibration showed a room with no atypical athlete would fire on 7-13. At 2.5 SD, zero flagged where chance predicts 1-2. Threshold was not retuned. 13 ADRs committed before the data was obtained; de-identified HTML report published | [[calibrate-the-threshold-against-a-null]] · [[when-you-are-your-own-reviewer-timestamp-the-threshold]] · [[vendor-percentiles-are-only-comparable-within-their-reference-group]] |

| 2026-07-17 | Applied Performance JD + semester OKRs | New job description accepted; OKR v3 restructured to semester cycles with mid-semester checkpoints | |
| 2026-07-08 | RTP joint presentation (deck + workbook) | 17-slide Eric+Jeremy Baylor return-to-play talk, act-when decision lines, QR-linked workbook | |
| 2026-06-17 | Morning-briefing pipeline | Automated daily email briefing with on-ramp distillation folded into `run.py`; survived + recovered from a 6-day silent venv outage | |
